div.head: Wi 20
div.ab: Gest hine clænsie sylfes aþe on wiofode; swylce cyninges ðeng;
Gest hine clænsie sylfes aþe on wiofode; swylce cyninges ðegn.
Gest hine clænsie sylfes aþe on wiofode; swylce cyninges ðe[gn].
Ein Fremder reinige sich durch Eid [nur] von [ihm] selbst auf dem Altar; ebenso ein Königsthegn.
A stranger is to clear himself by an oath of [him]self [alone] on the altar; likewise a king’s thegn.
A stranger shall clear himself by his own oath, at the altar. A king’s thegn [shall clear himself] in the same way.
A stranger is to purge himself with his own oath on the altar; similarly a king’s thegn;
A stranger should clear himself with his own oath at the altar; similarly the king’s thegn.

note.seg: swylce — weofode am unteren Rande, war anfangs vom Schreiber, den das gleiche Endwort verführt, übersprungen
swylce — weofode in the lower margin; at first skipped by the scribe, who was misled by the identical final word
‘Gast’ heisst im ältesten Germanisch auch der ungebetene Fremde; s. d. Gl 10
In the earliest Germanic, ‘guest’ also denotes the uninvited stranger; see that word in Gl 10

Dieselbe Metathese (Sievers Gramm. § 185) zeigt thengesshipe I Cn 6, 2a In⁵. — Der Eineid (s. d. Gl 1—2a) ist auch sonst Prozessvorrecht. Des Thegn (s. Gl 14) Eid gilt besonders hoch zwar auch später, bedarf jedoch der Helfer

The same metathesis (Sievers Gramm. § 185) appears in thengesshipe I Cn 6, 2a In⁵. — The sole oath (see that word in Gl 1—2a) is a procedural privilege elsewhere too. The thegn’s oath (see Gl 14) is indeed valued especially highly later as well, but it requires helpers

note.label: wiofode;
note.seg: Manuscript here has a symbol similar to ⁘ with a long descender extending into the right margin as an insertion mark; it is repeated before the words swylce … weofode which, inadvertently omitted, are written below the text at the bottom of the page.
